stories.headline: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows
stories.script: Our lead story today. Some artificial intelligence data centers are generating their own electricity with converted jet engines while they wait years for grid connections and new turbines, TechCrunch reports, citing the New York Times. The engines are taken from retired aircraft and rebuilt to run on natural gas. Nobody sees them as a long-term power source, but they show how far electricity supply has lagged behind the expansion of AI. For companies caught in those queues, the key appeal is how quickly the engines can be put to work. Audun Martinsen, an analyst at Rystad Energy, told the Times the priority is securing power as quickly as possible. He said jet-powered units can get a data center operating within 24 months. By comparison, the International Energy Agency says connecting 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia takes roughly seven years.

stories.headline: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
stories.script: Also today. Anthropic said in a blog post on Tuesday that it is developing an open source system to confirm which AI model generated a particular output. The system is named FlashProve. It aims to deliver what researchers describe as provable inference, meaning a cryptographic proof that acts as a mathematical guarantee that a response was produced by a specific model. The goal is to let users check that an answer genuinely came from the model they believe they are using. Cryptographic email signatures let recipients verify who really sent a message, and FlashProve works in a similar way. It is designed to stop anyone passing one model off as another, even if the deception comes from the lab that built and operates the model.

keyPoints: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity

stories.headline: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to 16 billion dollars as demand surges
stories.script: In other news. Fal, a San Francisco startup that operates and hosts models generating video, images and audio, has secured 1.3 billion dollars in new funding led by Bessemer Venture Partners. Nvidia, Sound Ventures and T also took part. According to Bloomberg, the deal values Fal at 16 billion dollars , twice the 8 billion dollars valuation it reached in April. Fal announced its Series E and Series F rounds together, saying the two brought in a combined 1.65 billion dollars . Sequoia led the earlier round. The latest raise, the Series F, comes as demand climbs for inference, which is the work of running an already trained AI model to produce outputs. That demand is especially strong among customers using open source models. Fal passed 800 million dollars in annualized revenue earlier this year, the report said.

stories.headline: ‘Discontent and distrust’: annual social cohesion checkup shows exactly what’s making Australia angry
stories.script: In Asia. Most Australians still support immigration and multiculturalism, even as more of them feel financially worse off and grow gloomier and more distrustful of government, the Guardian reports, citing the annual Scanlon report on social cohesion. Respondents are more anxious about artificial intelligence than about climate change or war. Their top worries, though, are a global economic slowdown and the cost of living. The report is among the nation's largest social research projects. It finds that financial strain is also changing how people vote, with those facing hardship shifting their support to One Nation. Concern about antisemitism and Islamophobia has grown, yet overall social cohesion has held steady. The report's lead author acknowledges that many of the findings are troubling.

stories.headline: IndiaAI Mission's three indigenous AI models target offline mobile access, secure use in critical sectors
stories.script: Turning to India. India's Union Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology on Tuesday launched three homegrown artificial intelligence models under the Foundation Model initiative of the IndiaAI Mission, the Economic Times reports. The models are named EKA-1, Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B, and they were built by Bengaluru-based Socket AI and ZenteiQ. Planned uses range from working offline on mobile phones to secure deployment in sensitive fields such as defence, cybersecurity and banking. The aim is to reduce India's reliance on foreign AI technology and meet the country's own requirements. ZenteiQ's Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B are small models that run directly on phones and need no internet connection. That is expected to bring AI services to people in places where connectivity is poor.

stories.headline: Albanese government warned it’s ‘sleepwalking into another robodebt scenario’ over use of algorithms and AI
stories.script: Around the world. An independent think tank has warned that Australia's federal government risks a repeat of the robodebt scandal, the Guardian reports. Dr Catherine Williams, chief executive of the Centre for Public Integrity, said the government was sleepwalking toward that outcome because there is little transparency and no legislation covering how algorithms and artificial intelligence shape official decisions. On Thursday she released the centre's report, titled Computer Says No. It reviews the government's reliance on automated decision-making tools and urges urgent reform. The centre fears Australians may not know when such systems have played a part in decisions about them. The report makes eight recommendations. They include a compulsory audit and a public register covering every use of automated decision-making, along with an independent watchdog with powers to monitor, audit and investigate the government.

stories.headline: Canva layoffs: design giant to cut or relocate more than 1,200 jobs in major restructure
stories.script: In other news. Australian-founded design company Canva will eliminate or move more than 1,200 roles, about 22 percent of its staff worldwide, in a sweeping overhaul, the Guardian reports. The company said 1,271 people will be affected as it works to remove management layers and bring more teams together in person. Among those leaving are employees who helped build the platform. In an email to staff on Wednesday, chief executive Melanie Perkins called the restructure "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history". She said some workers would see their roles change or be asked to move to central hubs, while others would be saying farewell to colleagues and friends. The move reflects a wider pattern across the technology industry. Software firms are trying to fend off lower-cost artificial intelligence challengers while building AI tools deeply into their own products.

stories.headline: AI ‘godfather’ Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
stories.script: Next. Geoffrey Hinton, one of the scientists often called the godfathers of artificial intelligence, has suggested humanity might have been better off if the technology had never been created, the Guardian reports. The 78-year-old Nobel prize-winning computer scientist's work on artificial neural networks underpins modern AI. He warned that a major incident could happen as soon as this year or next, such as a temporary shutdown of financial or power systems. Hinton told the paper he does not consider himself a doomer, and he believes AI could lead to a wonderful future. Still, he said that within a decade, and perhaps sooner, it will become clear whether humanity can control the risks. Success, he said, could bring what he called radical abundance.

stories.headline: Google says there’s no way to use Search without using artificial intelligence
stories.script: Elsewhere. Google has conceded that its search engine cannot be separated from artificial intelligence, the Guardian reports. On Tuesday the company unveiled a set of new AI products for schools, along with more ways for teachers and administrators to limit or block those tools. Google said schools should decide whether students use AI in class. There is a trade-off, though. If a school or teacher switches off Google's AI features, students also lose access to Google Search. In a blog post, company executives said they were revising controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search after consulting schools, teachers, researchers and policymakers. These products will stay fully disabled for K-12 student accounts until administrators actively enable them. Chris Phillips, Google's vice-president for education, told the New York Times that Google Search does not exist without AI.
stories.whyThisMatters: Google has conceded that its search engine cannot be separated from artificial intelligence, the Guardian reports.
keyPoints: Google says there’s no way to use Search without using artificial intelligence

stories.headline: Netflix’s new AI Discover tab helps you find something to watch based on your mood
stories.script: Turning to the United States. Netflix said on Tuesday it is introducing a new section called AI Discover, where viewers can try out new ways of choosing what to watch next. The first experimental feature in the section offers suggestions based on how a viewer is feeling at that moment. Users can pick from curated themes that feature clips from series and films. The themes are organized around mood, viewing tastes, how much time someone has, and titles that are new or trending. Options include something light, scare me, family movie night and quick watches. TechCrunch says the addition suggests Netflix wants to make its expanding catalogue simpler to browse. It points to a shift away from endless scrolling toward a more personalized way of finding programs, driven by artificial intelligence.
